lead: A power diode is a two-terminal semiconductor switch. In forward bias it conducts with a small voltage drop; in reverse bias it blocks with tiny leakage. Its static V–I curve gives the on-state drop and reverse current. Its switching curve shows charge stored in the junction during turn-off. This chapter defines static and dynamic characteristics, reverse recovery time, peak reverse current and charge. It compares the real diode with an ideal switch. Power diodes appear in rectifiers, choppers, inverters and AC controllers.
prereq: You need: the basic PN junction diode from semiconductor devices, including forward bias, reverse bias and the depletion region.

blocks.text: A power diode has three layers: a heavily doped p<sup>+</sup> anode, a lightly doped n<sup>−</sup> drift region, and a heavily doped n<sup>+</sup> cathode. The drift region is wide because it must support the reverse voltage. The anode is terminal A and the cathode is terminal K. The diode current is i<sub>D</sub> and the diode voltage is v<sub>D</sub>, positive from A to K.

In forward bias, v<sub>D</sub> must exceed a cut-in voltage V<sub>F</sub> before current rises sharply. For a silicon power diode, V<sub>F</sub> is roughly 0.8 V to 1.2 V, depending on current. Above cut-in, a useful model is v<sub>D</sub> = V<sub>F</sub> + i<sub>D</sub> r<sub>d</sub>, where r<sub>d</sub> is the slope resistance. In reverse bias, only a small reverse saturation current I<sub>S</sub> flows until avalanche breakdown at V<sub>BR</sub>.

An ideal switch has zero on-state voltage, infinite off-state resistance, zero switching time and no loss. A real diode fails all four: it has V<sub>F</sub>, finite r<sub>d</sub>, leakage I<sub>S</sub>, breakdown V<sub>BR</sub>, and stored charge that delays turn-off. The static curve is measured slowly, so it shows only conduction and blocking, not switching.

blocks.where: v<sub>D</sub> is forward diode voltage in volts (V); V<sub>F</sub> is cut-in voltage in volts (V); i<sub>D</sub> is forward current in amperes (A); r<sub>d</sub> is slope resistance in ohms (Ω).

blocks.text: Turn-on has a forward recovery time t<sub>fr</sub>. It is the delay from applying forward voltage until the diode reaches a specified forward drop. It is short in most power diodes. During this time, charge builds in the drift region and the voltage briefly overshoots.

Turn-off is slower because stored charge must be removed. When the external circuit reverses the current, the diode still conducts for a short time. The current crosses zero, reaches a peak reverse value I<sub>RRM</sub>, then returns to near zero after reverse recovery time t<sub>rr</sub>. The area under the reverse current is the reverse recovery charge Q<sub>rr</sub>. A triangular approximation gives Q<sub>rr</sub> = ½ I<sub>RRM</sub> t<sub>rr</sub>.

Split t<sub>rr</sub> into t<sub>a</sub>, from zero crossing to peak reverse current, and t<sub>b</sub>, from peak back to zero. The softness factor is S = t<sub>b</sub> / t<sub>a</sub>. A large S means gentle recovery and lower current slope. The average reverse-recovery loss is P<sub>rr</sub> = Q<sub>rr</sub> V<sub>s</sub> f<sub>s</sub>, where V<sub>s</sub> is the blocking voltage and f<sub>s</sub> is the switching frequency.

blocks.where: Q<sub>rr</sub> is reverse recovery charge in coulombs (C); I<sub>RRM</sub> is peak reverse recovery current in amperes (A); t<sub>rr</sub> is reverse recovery time in seconds (s).

P<sub>rr</sub> is average reverse-recovery power loss in watts (W); Q<sub>rr</sub> is charge in coulombs (C); V<sub>s</sub> is blocking voltage in volts (V); f<sub>s</sub> is switching frequency in hertz (Hz).

sections.h3: Diode types and where they sit

blocks.text: Power diodes are named by their recovery and conduction behaviour: standard recovery, fast-recovery and Schottky. Standard diodes are used at line frequency. Fast-recovery diodes are used when switching is fast. Schottky diodes have a low forward drop and very short recovery, but lower voltage ratings.

A one-line map of converters: a rectifier changes AC to DC, a chopper changes DC to DC, an inverter changes DC to AC, and an AC controller changes AC to AC. The circuits belong to later units. See Unit 2, Controlled and Uncontrolled Rectifiers for diode rectifiers, and Unit 3, DC-DC Converters for choppers. See Unit 4, DC-AC Inverters and Unit 5, AC-AC Converters for the other two.

figure.caption: The diode carries 10 A, then current reverses to a peak of −8 A and returns to zero over about 2 μs. The negative area is the reverse recovery charge removed at turn-off.

spec.aria: Diode current stays at 10 A until 2 μs, falls to a peak reverse value of −8 A at 2.2 μs, and recovers to zero at 4 μs.

examples.question: A diode carries 10 A. Its reverse recovery time is 2 μs and its peak reverse recovery current is 8 A. Treat the recovery charge as a triangle and find Q<sub>rr</sub>. If the diode blocks 300 V and switches at 20 kHz, find the average reverse-recovery power loss using P<sub>rr</sub> = Q<sub>rr</sub> V<sub>s</sub> f<sub>s</sub>.
steps: Use the triangular charge model: Q<sub>rr</sub> = ½ × I<sub>RRM</sub> × t<sub>rr</sub>.
Put I<sub>RRM</sub> = 8 A and t<sub>rr</sub> = 2 μs = 2 × 10<sup>−6</sup> s.
Use V<sub>s</sub> = 300 V and f<sub>s</sub> = 20 kHz = 20 × 10<sup>3</sup> Hz.
examples.check:
I_RRM = 8
t_rr_us = 2
Q_uC = 0.5 * I_RRM * t_rr_us
V_s = 300
f_s_kHz = 20
P_W = Q_uC * 1e-6 * V_s * f_s_kHz * 1e3
print(Q_uC)
print(P_W)

traps: Do not add t<sub>rr</sub> to turn-on time. Reverse recovery is a turn-off effect.
Q<sub>rr</sub> is charge in coulombs or microcoulombs, not current. I<sub>RRM</sub> is the current peak.
The softness factor is S = t<sub>b</sub> / t<sub>a</sub>, not the total recovery time.
Cut-in voltage V<sub>F</sub> is not the full on-state voltage at high current; include the i<sub>D</sub> r<sub>d</sub> term.

quiz.q: Define reverse recovery time t<sub>rr</sub> of a power diode.
quiz.a: t<sub>rr</sub> is the time from the current crossing zero during turn-off until the reverse current has fallen to a specified small value near zero.

quiz.q: State four properties of an ideal switch.
quiz.a: Zero on-state voltage, infinite off-state resistance, zero switching time, and zero loss.

quiz.q: Why does a diode still carry reverse current for a short time after the circuit tries to turn it off?
quiz.a: Charge stored in the drift region must be removed. Until that charge is swept out or recombined, the junction cannot block, so reverse current flows.

quiz.q: A diode has I<sub>RRM</sub> = 6 A and t<sub>rr</sub> = 3 μs. Treat recovery as a triangle. Find Q<sub>rr</sub>.
For the diode above, V<sub>s</sub> = 200 V and f<sub>s</sub> = 25 kHz. Find P<sub>rr</sub>.
What does a large softness factor S mean for the turn-off current waveform?
quiz.a: A large S means t<sub>b</sub> is larger than t<sub>a</sub>. The current falls gently after the reverse peak, so the current slope is smaller and voltage spikes and EMI are usually lower.

quiz.q: Compare a real power diode with an ideal switch in a chopper.
quiz.a: The real diode has forward drop V<sub>F</sub> and slope resistance r<sub>d</sub>, so it loses conduction power. It has leakage and breakdown limits, and it has reverse recovery charge, so it loses switching power and limits high-frequency operation. The ideal switch has none of these losses or delays.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, diode reverse recovery is often the reason a converter needs a snubber or a soft-switching tank. Device makers publish Q<sub>rr</sub>, t<sub>rr</sub> and softness factor on datasheets because these numbers decide EMI and switching loss. Wide band-gap diodes such as SiC Schottky have almost no reverse recovery, so they are used in fast chargers and solar inverters. Search next for “diode reverse recovery charge”, “soft recovery diode” and “SiC Schottky diode”.
